text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Consent-based, trauma-informed care at every visit: explain each examination, test and procedure beforehand (what it is, why, what it involves, the alternatives, including not doing it), ask her agreement and record it, offer a chaperone or companion of her choosing, let her stop at any time, never perform an unplanned procedure, and keep the plan in writing; written consent for any procedure beyond routine tests
  • Nephrology consultation by telehealth from the health center, with the community health worker present, for albumin in the urine and reduced kidney function in a woman with an old kidney injury, new diabetes and high blood pressure readings
  • Blood pressure: a validated home monitor with a large cuff, provided by the health center, with readings twice a day for seven days to confirm the diagnosis; less salt, using foods she can get; recheck in two weeks
  • Diabetes: metformin extended-release once daily, an A1c every three months until at goal, diabetes self-management education in a group class at the health center, and no medicine that can cause low blood sugar
  • Kidneys: repeat the urine albumin test, a kidney ultrasound with the consultation, no ibuprofen or naproxen, and kidney function and potassium checks after any blood pressure or kidney medicine is started
  • Cardiovascular risk: atorvastatin 40 mg with a lipid panel at four to twelve weeks, a baseline ECG, and TSH at diagnosis
  • Eyes and feet: retinal photographs in the clinic, so that no separate trip is needed; a comprehensive foot examination yearly; daily foot checks at home, callus care at the health center and well-fitting shoes
  • Social needs, with the community health worker: the AHC health-related social needs screen at intake and every few months; help applying for SNAP and the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program; the health center's food pantry and produce program; 211 for other local help; rides arranged for every visit and laboratory test; the sliding-fee scale; 90-day medicine supplies at the discount pharmacy, and phone visits when travel is not possible
  • Shared decisions and the team: Dr. Batiste-Hill, a nurse, the community health worker and the pharmacist review the plan with her; medicines chosen for cost, once-daily dosing and her preferences; she decides what she accepts
  • Mood and stress: PHQ-9 at intake and at four months, asked privately; counseling offered at her choice
  • Vaccines: pneumococcal, hepatitis B and Tdap offered, explained and given only with her agreement; influenza and COVID-19 each autumn
  • On the consultant's advice: amlodipine 5 mg with benazepril 20 mg in one daily capsule and dapagliflozin 10 mg daily with sick-day rules; potassium and creatinine one to two weeks after starting; urine albumin again at three to four months; blood pressure goal below 130/80; review of kidney treatment by telehealth if albumin stays raised
  • Laboratory checks on the days she is already at the health center, with a ride arranged in advance for any extra check; home blood draw by the mobile phlebotomy service when no ride can be found
  • Metformin extended-release increased to 1,500 mg with the evening meal, because the A1c was still above goal

resource.title: Fannie Lou Hamer synthetic care plan
resource.description: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes and kidney disease in a 49-year-old community organizer in the rural Mississippi Delta, managed at a community health center with trauma-informed care. The teaching contrast is her documented sterilization without consent: here every examination, test and procedure is explained beforehand, done only with her documented consent, with a chaperone of her choosing, and stopped or declined at her word without loss of care. The episode covers confirming hypertension with home readings under the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline, diagnosing and treating diabetes under the ADA Standards of Care 2026, kidney function and urine albumin with KDIGO, an ACE inhibitor and an SGLT2 inhibitor, a statin, retinal photographs, foot care, medication choices for cost and adherence, a community health worker on the team, a social needs screen with real resources for food, transportation and utility costs, shared decisions, and preventive care.
